title: Active verbs and the N- prefix
title_target: Tuku dadi nuku, pangan dadi mangan
goal: Form active verbs with the nasal prefix N- — the one piece of Javanese word-building you truly have to learn, and simpler than it looks.
bekal: turn a root word into an active verb with N-
recognize the root behind a verb that already carries the prefix
use everyday verbs in ngoko and krama

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Resik-resik ing kos
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning. Rini is sweeping the porch; Dian has just woken up. A ngoko conversation packed with prefixed verbs — count how many roots you can spot.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Wis tangi? Aku wiwit nyapu ket mau ésuk.
lines.id: Up already? I've been sweeping since early this morning.
lines.literal: already wake? I start sweep since earlier morning.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aduh, aku turu kebablasen. Tak réwangi, ya.
lines.id: Oh no, I overslept. I'll help you.
lines.literal: oh-no, I sleep overshot. I help, yeah.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ora usah. Kowé ngumbah klambimu waé, wis numpuk kaé.
lines.id: No need. Just wash your clothes — they're piling up over there.
lines.literal: not need. you wash clothes-your just, already pile that.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya. Mengko aku uga arep masak lan nyuci piring.
lines.id: OK. Later I'm also going to cook and do the dishes.
lines.literal: yes. later I also will cook and wash plate.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Apik. Aku arep maca buku sedhéla, sésuk ana ujian.
lines.id: Good. I'm going to read for a bit — I have an exam tomorrow.
lines.literal: good. I will read book a-moment, tomorrow there-is exam.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Kowé sinau nganti bengi terus, ya?
lines.id: You always study till late at night, don't you?
lines.literal: you study until night continuously, yeah?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Kepeksa. Bèn ora nggarap tugas dadakan.
lines.id: I have to. So I'm not doing assignments at the last minute.
lines.literal: forced. so-that not work-on assignment sudden.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: Shall I get you some water?

notes: **Ket** is the short form of *wiwit* (since, starting from). Krama is also *wiwit*. You'll often hear *ket mau* (since earlier), *ket wingi* (since yesterday).
**Kebablasen** — a very Javanese word meaning "to overshoot": oversleep, miss your stop, go too far. The ending *-en* here marks something that happens to you without meaning to.
**Ora usah** means "no need"; krama *boten sisah*. It's the usual way to turn down help or an offer. Even softer: *mboten, matur nuwun* (no, thank you).
**Bèn** means "so that"; krama *supados*. On its own it can also mean "let it be, never mind": *bèn waé* (just leave it).

**Njupukké** is *njupuk* (to take) plus the ending *-ké*, meaning "to do something for someone": *njupukké* (fetch for), *tukokké* (buy for), *gawèkké* (make for). Compare English "get *me* some water". More in Unit 18.

**Kepeksa** (forced to) uses the prefix *ke-*, which marks something that happens to you against your will: *ketiban* (be hit by a falling object), *kesasar* (get lost), *keturon* (fall asleep by accident).

grammars.title: The N- prefix: one prefix, six faces
body: Grammar books write the Javanese active prefix as **N-**, but it never actually appears as the letter N. It takes on the nasal sound that matches the first letter of the root — a bit like English *in-* becoming *im-* in *impossible*. The difference: Javanese often **drops** the root's first letter.
after: The pattern is actually simple: **voiceless letters (p, t, k, s, w) drop and are replaced by their nasal**; **voiced letters (b, d, j, g) stay, with the nasal in front**. Say *m-b*, *n-d*, *ng-g* aloud and you'll feel why: the nasal and the voiced stop sit in the same place in the mouth.
**Roots that already begin with a nasal don't change**: *mangan* can't take another nasal, nor can *ngerti*.

Your hardest job isn't **building** verbs but **taking them apart**: when you look up *nulis* in a dictionary and can't find it, remember the root is *tulis*. *Maca* → *waca*. *Mangan* → *pangan*. *Nyilih* → *silih*. This habit is what makes a Javanese dictionary usable.

blocks.text: This table is the backbone of everyday conversation. Look at the krama column: most krama verbs are **completely different words**, not variations of the ngoko. That's why they have to be learned in pairs.

blocks.title: Krama inggil: who is it for?
items: **Krama** lowers yourself; **krama inggil** raises the other person. So you use *nedha* for what you do, and *dhahar* for what someone you respect does.
*Kula sampun nedha* — I've eaten. *Bapak sampun dhahar?* — Have you eaten, sir? Swapping them is the mistake people notice instantly: saying *kula dhahar* means elevating yourself.
At A1, just learn the five most common: **dhahar** (eat), **tindak** (go), **saré** (sleep), **ngendika** (speak), **pirsa** (know). You'll hear all five from older people every day.

blocks.text: Not every verb takes a prefix. Most verbs describing a **state** or the **doer's own movement** are used as they are, without N-:
Some of these **look** prefixed (*mlaku*, *mlayu*, *mangan*), but the prefix has fused and no longer feels like one to native speakers. Don't think about it; just learn the forms in use.

blocks.title: Adus, siram, and the danger of the wrong level
items: *Adus* (ngoko) → *siram* (krama). *Bapak sampun siram?* means "Have you had your bath, sir?" — a normal morning question.
But in ngoko *siram* also means "to water (plants)". Context tells them apart, and context is almost always enough.
Don't ask *Bapak wis adus?* to someone much older. Ngoko for the actions of someone you respect sounds like talking to a small child.

exercises.prompt: Turn these roots into active verbs with the N- prefix.
Now the other way round: write the root of each verb.

items: Rini reads a book every night.
Do you want to get some water?
I haven't washed my clothes yet.

exercises.prompt: **Review of Unit 6.** Cover Unit 6, then write the Javanese sentences.
items: Tomorrow I'm going to the market. (krama)
Yesterday I didn't go to class. (ngoko)
